                                         I. Routing Considerations

         The over-arching issue in this matter is which transmission line route is the best route when

considering and weighing the factors set forth in PURA § 37.056(c) and TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B).

Pursuant to PURA § 37.056(c) and TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B), Applicants evaluated and weighed

thirty-six (36) criteria and provided data regarding the same. While no single factor controls or is

dispositive, the PUC is directed to reasonably consider all the various factors and their impact.9

However, notably, length, cost, and habitable structures tend to be viewed by the PUC as important

factors.10 The chart attached hereto as Exhibit “A” depicts how Routes 392, 487, 894, and 894

(Western Mod 1) compare when considering all thirty-six (36) routing criteria Applicants factored

into their routing decision.

         When considering and weighing the factors, the record makes clear that Route 894 or Route

487 as a whole best satisfy PURA § 37.056(c) and TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B) and, for the following

reasons, either Route 894 or Route 487 should be selected by the PUC for the construction of the

transmission line.

         The parties supporting Routes 392 and 894 (Western Mod 1) focus heavily on the following

factors in their initial briefs: community values, cost, historical significance, aesthetics,

environmental integrity, engineering constraints, and paralleling of existing rights-of-way.

Therefore, this Reply Brief addresses those same concerns.11

 A.      Community Values

        As stated in the N12/P1 Intervenors’ Initial Post-Hearing Brief, there appears to be one

community value shared across the entire study area: no landowner wants the proposed

transmission line constructed on their property. Regardless of where the transmission line is

constructed, some landowners will be negatively affected.12 The N12/P1 Intervenors agree and

concede this is true.

        Several intervenors have pointed to the number of parties supporting or opposing a given

link or route as strong evidence of community values.13 For example, one intervenor group

includes a table in their brief identifying landowners who do not oppose a particular route.14 First,

this is irrelevant because, at most, it merely states the obvious: landowners generally do not oppose

routes that do not affect their land.15 Second, this is nothing more than an attempt to turn the routing

selection process into a popularity contest. The Link R1 Opposition Landowners similarly rely on

the intervenor map as evidence that certain links are more opposed and that certain communities

are more opposed to the proposed transmission line.16 But the number and location of intervenors

is an unreliable and inherently skewed metric. There are many reasons why individuals may

choose or not choose to intervene: Did they receive notice? Could they afford the expense of

litigating the route? Given the number of attorneys in this case who would have conflicts, could

they find someone to represent them? Moreover, variables like population density and tract size

necessarily influence the number of intervenors associated with any given link or route. For these

         In their initial briefs, the Brady Creek Intervenors, the Segment K13/K51 Landowners, and

others point to long lists of experts who purport to share their respective routing preferences.18

While these experts may provide insight on the routing criteria, these experts are merely witnesses

who are paid to offer an opinion favorable to the parties who hired them. These paid “experts”

should not be afforded greater weight than the testimony of landowners who have a personal stake

in this case.

         Route 392

         As further discussed in this Reply Brief and previously laid out in detail in the N12/P1

runoff, dominating views, crossing cattle pens and pastures, and impacting creeks that these

properties depend on.20 While these may be legitimate concerns for the Brady Creek Intervenors,

uncertain, future development.25 The PUC affords no weight to future development.26

        Route 894 (Western Mod 1)

        Route 894 (Western Mod 1) should be recognized for what it is: a self-serving attempt to

avoid the properties of the Link R1 Opposition Landowners. As referred to during the Hearing on

the Merits as an “RFI route,” Route 894 (Western Mod 1) is a route developed by landowners for

the sole purpose of diverting the proposed transmission line away from their own land.27 The origin

principled application of the PUC’s routing criteria.

        It is equally telling that, among the 1,246 routes included in the Application, the

        The Link R1 Opposition Landowners (and others) attempt to justify their proposal of Route

community values throughout McCulloch and Concho Counties that favor industrial

development.29 However, the values of a single property owner do not reflect those of the

community members whose properties would be burdened by the proposed transmission line.

Moreover, there is no evidence that the wind farm is located on any property owned by the N12/P1

Intervenors. In effect, the Link R1 Opposition Landowners seek to penalize the N12/P1 Intervenors

control.

        The Link R1 Opposition Landowners reliance on the Pfluger Family Limited Partnership’s

(“Pfluger FLP”) option agreements is similarly misplaced. While Pfluger FLP executed wind

Link R1 Opposition Landowners attempt to spin these agreements pertaining to other property as

evidence of “community value” favoring the use of Link P1.31 The record simply does not support

that leap.

         The proponents of Route 392 do not address historical and archeological values in their

brief.38 Similarly, the proponents of Route 894 (Western Mod 1), Link R1 Opposition Landowners,

hardly touch these topics.39 But, who can blame them? With regard to historical effects, Routes

392 and 894 (Western Mod 1) utterly fail in comparison to Route 894.

        Route 392

        When compared to Route 894, Route 392 crosses 14 more cultural resource sites, has 35

more cultural resource sites within 1,000 feet of the Proposed Transmission Line, and is 10.6 miles

longer across high value historical or archeological lands.40

        Dr. Turnbough, who testified on behalf of and was hired by the Brady Creek Intervenors,

stated that shifting the transmission line to the northern edge of the study area (as in Route 392)

moves “away from fragmentation of historic and high quality ranches located in the central

corridor . . . .”41 However, this generalized assertion fails to account for the impact Route 392

would have on the historic and cultural resources located on Route 392. The Brady Creek

Intervenors are willing to sacrifice the “historic and high quality ranches” on Route 392 to avoid

Route 894.42

foreground visual zone of parks and recreational area than Route 894.43 Also, Route 392 parallels

more state and federal highway than Route 894 by 16.32 miles.44 While there is some benefit from

        As noted above, the Link R1 Opposition Landowners argue that the transmission line

for miles, including from their own properties. Any claim that their views of the surrounding

landscape are unblemished is disingenuous at best. Finally, while a small portion of the proposed

route may traverse the wind farm, the Link R1 Opposition Landowners fail to account for the

substantial stretches of otherwise undeveloped property that would also be crossed by the

transmission line.

                                         III.    Conclusion

Staff's "best meets" Route 487 satisfy the factors set forth in PURA § 37.056(c) and TAC §

evidence also points to Route 894 being the superior route. Attached to this Brief as Exhibit "A"
